sources.title: My claim about Isaiah 53 is “demonstrably false”?
sources.author: Dan McClellan
sources.summary: McClellan reads the servant as Israel and its suffering as exile. He distinguishes a messianic reading from a reading about a suffering, dying Messiah. Page’s cited conclusion leaves earlier developments possible, while questioning claims of a fully developed expectation.

sources.title: What is Deutero-Isaiah?
sources.author: Dan McClellan
sources.summary: Deutero-Isaiah means Second Isaiah, the scholarly name for Isaiah 40–55. McClellan explains the case for composition centuries after the eighth-century prophet. sources.title: Does the Great Isaiah Scroll prove the Bible hasn’t changed?

sources.author: William A. Tooman
sources.year: 2021 · in Isaiah’s Servants in Early Judaism and Christianity
sources.summary: Tooman compares the traditional Hebrew text with the Isaiah Targum. The Targum presents a victorious Messiah who protects those who suffer. lds.text: Meridian study question: How do physical restoration and return to God support each other in this vision? Read the linked Come, Follow Me lesson for the Church study perspective.

passages.title: The Assyrian crisis
passages.summary: Assyria captures Judah’s fortified towns. An Assyrian official then travels from Lachish to confront Jerusalem. Assyrian palace reliefs also show Lachish.
passages.dateLabel: 701 BCE · campaign setting
passages.uncertainty: The campaign took place in 701 BCE. The map connects the cities named in the passage. The exact route is unknown.

lds.text: Read Hezekiah’s crisis as an invitation to trust God while facing a real political danger. Church teaching treats the historical setting as the background for that spiritual question.

passages.title: A battle over trust
passages.summary: The Assyrian speaker challenges trust in Egypt, Hezekiah, and Judah’s God. He speaks to the people on the wall. He promises food but also describes moving them to another land.
passages.dateLabel: 701 BCE · narrative setting
passages.uncertainty: Isaiah records these speeches as part of the account. No separate record from the campaign confirms their exact words.

lds.text: The repeated question of whom to trust can be read alongside Hezekiah’s leadership. Condie’s conference talk applies his example to communities choosing change. Related Come, Follow Me lesson (2026): The lesson on Isaiah 7–9 emphasizes trust in the Lord during political pressure. Meridian study question: How does Ahaz’s challenge compare with the appeals for trust in Isaiah 36? Related general conference study: Rowe uses Isaiah 41:10 and 43:1, 3 to discuss trust when fear arises. Meridian study question: How does this counsel relate to the threats in Isaiah 36?

passages.title: The letter and the prayer
passages.summary: Hezekiah takes the threatening message to the temple. His prayer names Assyria’s victories and declares that Judah’s God is the Creator.
passages.dateLabel: 701 BCE · narrative setting
passages.uncertainty: The passage explains the events through faith in God. It does not provide separate historical proof of how Jerusalem survived.

lds.text: Hezekiah’s prayer offers a faithful model for turning toward God in distress. This is a devotional reading of the narrative, alongside the evidence discussed in Historical mode. Related Come, Follow Me lesson (2026): The lesson on Isaiah 40–49 emphasizes God’s strength over worldly powers. Meridian study question: How does that theme compare with Hezekiah’s prayer to the Creator in Isaiah 37:16–20?

passages.title: Jerusalem survives
passages.summary: Isaiah compares the survivors to a plant that takes root again. His account credits God with saving Jerusalem. Assyrian accounts describe a royal victory.
passages.dateLabel: 701 BCE · main crisis
passages.uncertainty: The sources give different explanations. The app cannot confirm the exact battle route or the number of deaths.

lds.text: LDS teaching reads the city’s preservation as an expression of God’s power to deliver. The remnant image also invites reflection on renewal after devastation.

passages.title: A later death closes the story
passages.summary: The chapter ends with Sennacherib’s death in his own land. Many years pass between his return home and his death.
passages.dateLabel: 681 BCE · later aftermath
passages.uncertainty: This verse should not be dated to the same night or year as the 701 BCE crisis.

lds.text: A faithful reading sees the ending as fulfillment of the earlier prophecy. The timeline shows the years between these events.

passages.title: Illness and a sign
passages.summary: Hezekiah becomes ill. God promises to save him and the city. Verse 6 shows why chapter order may differ from the order of events.
passages.dateLabel: Around the Assyrian crisis · date uncertain
passages.uncertainty: The map uses 701 BCE to show the setting. The date of Hezekiah’s illness is uncertain.

lds.text: The Lord’s promise to hear prayer offers hope in times of need. Hezekiah’s recovery does not promise the same outcome for every illness. Related Come, Follow Me lesson (2026): The lesson on Isaiah 53 emphasizes Christ’s bearing of human grief. Meridian study question: How does hope in the Savior relate to Hezekiah’s distress? His recovery does not promise healing for everyone. Related general conference study: Andersen uses Isaiah 61:3 to offer hope after suffering, without setting a time for healing. Meridian study question: How does this help distinguish hope in Christ from a promise of immediate recovery?

passages.title: Hezekiah’s song after recovery
passages.summary: The poem moves through images of Sheol, a tent, a loom, birds, and the pit. It ends with living people praising God and passing faithfulness to their children.
passages.dateLabel: Hezekiah’s lifetime · exact date unknown
passages.uncertainty: The poem appears in Isaiah 38, but its exact date is unknown. The map shows Jerusalem as its setting.

lds.text: Church teaching uses this passage to discuss suffering, mercy, and forgiveness. The poem offers ideas for reflection. It does not promise physical recovery for everyone. Related Come, Follow Me lesson (2026): The lesson connects Isaiah 61:1–3 with the Savior’s healing mission. Meridian study question: How does its change from mourning to joy compare with Hezekiah’s song after recovery? Related general conference study: Matswagothata uses Isaiah 40:31 to discuss renewed strength during trials. Meridian study question: How does this compare with Hezekiah’s gratitude for restored life?

passages.title: Babylon and Judah’s future
passages.summary: Visitors from Babylon meet Hezekiah. Isaiah warns that Babylon will later take the palace wealth and the king’s descendants. McClellan’s authorship overview contrasts this warning of exile with the exile already assumed in Isaiah 40. He presents this shift as evidence for later composition of Isaiah 40–55, often called Second Isaiah.
passages.dateLabel: Late eighth century BCE · embassy date debated
passages.uncertainty: The map uses 703 BCE to show the setting. The visit’s exact date is uncertain. Chapter order does not prove the visit followed the 701 BCE crisis. Select 597 or 587/586 BCE to study later events.

lds.text: The Church manual reads these chapters as a transition from Assyrian danger to Babylonian captivity. Consider the contrast between present security and responsibility for future generations. Related Come, Follow Me lesson (2026): The lesson on Isaiah 13–14 treats Babylon as a symbol of pride. Meridian study question: How does that theme relate to Hezekiah’s display of wealth in Isaiah 39? Also consider the visitors as people in their historical setting.

passages.title: Comfort and renewed strength

passages.title: Humility, comfort, and all nations
passages.summary: The LORD values humility above claims based on a temple alone. Zion's sudden birth and maternal comfort accompany judgment. The book ends with gathered nations, continuing worship, and a severe picture of rebellion's outcome.
passages.dateLabel: Literary context · no assigned event year

events.title: Before the crisis
events.summary: Judah and Israel face the growing power of Assyria. This date shows the earlier setting. It does not mark one event.
events.uncertainty: 780 BCE marks the pilot’s chosen viewing boundary, not Isaiah’s birth or a campaign.

events.title: The northern kingdom falls
events.summary: The speaker in Isaiah 36 uses Samaria’s defeat as a warning. Assyria took the city, faced another revolt, and strengthened its control.
events.uncertainty: 722/721 BCE refers to several stages of conquest and control. Scholars differ on the dates of these stages.

events.title: A new Assyrian king
events.summary: Sargon II dies and Sennacherib succeeds him. Subject states contest Assyrian power.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Babylon challenges Assyria
events.summary: Sennacherib defeats Merodach-baladan in Babylonia, providing context for the ruler named in Isaiah 39.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Sennacherib’s western campaign
events.summary: The Assyrian campaign reaches Judah. Compare the narrative, the royal inscriptions, and the Lachish reliefs.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Palace reliefs show Lachish
events.summary: The palace reliefs present the conquest for an Assyrian royal audience. The artifact was made after the event it depicts.
events.uncertainty: 695 BCE is a display position within the museum’s dating range of 700–692 BCE.

events.title: Sennacherib’s reign ends
events.summary: The later death at the end of Isaiah 37 extends the narrative beyond the invasion year.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Nineveh falls
events.summary: The fall of Nineveh weakens Assyrian power. Some Assyrian forces continue to resist.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Babylon gains power in the west
events.summary: The battle at Carchemish helps Babylon gain power in the eastern Mediterranean region.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Jerusalem and royal deportation
events.summary: Babylon captures Jerusalem and takes its king into exile. These later events help explain the warning in Isaiah 39.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

events.title: Jerusalem and the temple destroyed
events.summary: Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple. This event occurs long after the Assyrian crisis.
events.uncertainty: Scholars date the destruction to 587 or 586 BCE. The app shows both dates.

events.title: Persia takes Babylon
events.summary: Cyrus conquers Babylon. The Cyrus Cylinder describes his support for restoring worship. It does not mention the return of Judah’s exiles.
events.uncertainty: The year helps place the event in time. Map routes and areas are approximate.

campaigns.title: From Lachish to Jerusalem
campaigns.summary: Isaiah 36:2 sends the Assyrian representative from Lachish to Jerusalem. The connection brings the campaign to the city’s walls.
campaigns.detail: The line connects Lachish and Jerusalem. The passage does not establish the official’s exact road or travel time. It does not trace Sennacherib’s movements. Compare the chapter with the Assyrian reliefs of Lachish.
campaigns.uncertainty: The line connects places in the account. The exact route is unknown.

campaigns.title: The Assyrian campaign in the west
campaigns.summary: A regional view of places affected by the western campaign before the confrontation at Jerusalem.
campaigns.detail: The royal account describes victories and defeated rulers. The map connects places to show the region. It does not confirm travel through every stop.
campaigns.uncertainty: The order of stops and the route are approximate.

campaigns.title: The Babylonian embassy
campaigns.dateLabel: Late eighth century BCE · exact date debated
campaigns.summary: Isaiah 39 links Babylonian visitors with Hezekiah’s court.
campaigns.detail: The curve connects Babylon and Jerusalem through the north. The passage does not establish this route or the visit’s exact year.
campaigns.uncertainty: The line connects the two cities. The travel route and exact date are unknown.

campaigns.title: Exile in Babylon
campaigns.summary: Compare Jerusalem and Babylon to study the later events described in Isaiah 39.
campaigns.detail: The map connects Jerusalem and Babylon. The line does not show one confirmed route into exile. People did not travel continuously throughout this period.
campaigns.uncertainty: The line connects the cities. The exact route into exile is unknown.

regions.name: Babylonia · approximate regional influence
regions.summary: The shaded area marks Babylonia around Babylon and the southern river plains. Local rulers and Assyrian kings contested power here.
regions.uncertainty: This shape provides regional context, not exact borders or continuous independent rule. Sennacherib defeated Merodach-baladan in 703 BCE. The later empire appears from 605 BCE.

regions.name: Judah · regional focus
regions.summary: The shaded area shows Judah’s hill country and nearby lowlands.
regions.uncertainty: The area is approximate. Borders and local control varied.

regions.name: Assyrian influence · approximate
regions.summary: The shaded area shows approximate Assyrian influence. Assyria governed some areas directly. Other rulers paid tribute.
regions.uncertainty: The area of influence changed over time. The shape does not show exact yearly borders or equal control in all areas.

regions.name: Babylonian influence · approximate
regions.summary: The shaded area shows approximate Babylonian influence after the Assyrian crisis.
regions.uncertainty: The area of influence is approximate. Select the area to see its sources.

regions.name: Persian transition · regional focus
regions.summary: The final frame marks the transfer of Babylon to Persian rule.
regions.uncertainty: Regional focus only; not the complete borders of Cyrus’s empire.

words.label: King
words.meaning: A ruler. The verse names both Judah’s king and the Assyrian king.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H4428. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: Both rulers have the title king, but their power differs. Later, the speaker calls the Assyrian king “great” to stress his power.

words.label: Hezekiah
words.meaning: The king of Judah in this account.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H2396. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.

words.label: Sennacherib
words.meaning: The Assyrian king named at the opening of the campaign narrative.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H5576. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.

words.label: Assyria
words.meaning: The empire that threatens Judah.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H804. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: The Hebrew names Assyria, while the Greek phrase calls its ruler king of the Assyrians. Both identify the power attacking Judah.

words.label: Judah
words.meaning: The southern kingdom in this passage.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H3063. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: Elsewhere, Judah can name an ancestor, a people, or a territory. Here the references to cities and Jerusalem identify the kingdom.

words.label: Rabshakeh
words.meaning: An Assyrian official’s title. The translation uses an English spelling of its sounds.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H7262. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: Strong’s Hebrew dictionary explains the title Rabshakeh as “chief cupbearer,” an official who served drinks to the king. In Isaiah 36, this official speaks for the Assyrian king and urges Jerusalem to surrender. Here, his role is that of a senior royal representative.

words.label: Lachish
words.meaning: A fortified city of Judah; the starting point of the mission to Jerusalem.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H3923. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.

words.label: Jerusalem
words.meaning: Judah’s royal and temple city.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H3389. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: In Isaiah 36:2, the Hebrew word has an ending that means toward Jerusalem. English expresses this direction with the separate word “to.”

words.label: Army
words.meaning: A military force in this context.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H2426. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: The Hebrew word can mean force or strength. Here it refers to soldiers sent by the king. The Greek word can also mean power or force.

words.label: Aqueduct
words.meaning: A channel that carries water.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H8585. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.

words.label: Pool
words.meaning: A water pool or reservoir.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H1295. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.

words.label: Confidence
words.greekNote: Swete’s text uses πεποιθὼς in verse 4. This verb form expresses trust in a question. It is not a direct noun match for “confidence.”
words.meaning: The reliance or confidence that the speaker challenges.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H986. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: In Isaiah 36:4, the Hebrew noun for confidence and the related verb for trust occur in the same question. This repetition introduces the speech’s repeated challenge: whom can Judah trust?

words.label: Trust
words.greekNote: This form comes from verse 5. The Greek verb has different forms elsewhere in the chapter.
words.meaning: To rely on someone or something.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H982. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: Rabshakeh challenges trust in Egypt’s military help in Isaiah 36:6, 9 and trust in the LORD’s rescue in verse 15. His speech attacks both reasons for resisting Assyria.

words.label: Egypt
words.meaning: The southern power whose help the speaker depicts as unreliable.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H4714. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: The Assyrian speaker compares Egypt to a broken reed. He uses this image to argue that Egypt cannot help Judah.

words.label: Aramaic
words.greekNote: The Greek adverb Συριστί names the language. Its ancient meaning differs from modern national names.
words.meaning: The language the Judean officials ask the envoy to use.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H762. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: The officials ask for Aramaic so the people on the wall cannot understand the discussion. The speaker continues in the people’s language.

words.label: Jews’ language
words.meaning: In Judean: the speech of the local audience, rendered “the Jews’ language” in WEB.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H3066. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: One Hebrew adverb corresponds to the English phrase “the Jews’ language.” In Isaiah 36:13, Rabshakeh uses this language to address the people on the wall directly.

words.label: Remnant
words.greekNote: This Greek form comes from verse 4 and means those left. Verse 32 uses another form. Verse 31 uses different Hebrew wording and has no match in this entry.
words.meaning: Those remaining after disaster or loss.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H7611. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: In Isaiah 37:4, Hezekiah asks for prayer for the survivors. In verses 31–32, roots and fruit describe their future recovery. The image presents survival as the beginning of renewed life.

words.label: Spirit
words.meaning: A spirit or state of mind that God says he will put in the Assyrian king.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H7307. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: The Hebrew word can mean wind, breath, or spirit. Isaiah 37:7 connects it with the Assyrian king hearing news and returning home.

words.label: Shadow
words.meaning: The shadow involved in the sign given to Hezekiah.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H6738. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.

words.label: Steps / sundial
words.meaning: Steps or degrees. Some translations use “sundial” for the structure where the shadow appears.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H4609. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: The World English Bible translates wording about steps as “sundial.” The Hebrew does not specify a circular clock face.

words.label: Sheol
words.meaning: The realm or place of the dead in the poem’s imagery.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H7585. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: Isaiah 38:18–19 contrasts the dead, who cannot praise God, with the living, who can. Hezekiah places his own praise within that contrast after his rescue from death.

related.label: Matthew 16:18 — gates of Hades
related.note: A later verbal/image comparison, not a claim that Matthew directly quotes Isaiah 38.

words.label: Soul / life
words.meaning: The speaker’s life or self, rescued from destruction.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H5315. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: Isaiah 38:17 places rescue from death beside forgiveness of sins. The reference to his soul belongs to Hezekiah’s thanks for his restored life.

words.label: Sins
words.meaning: Wrongdoing that the poem describes as thrown behind God’s back.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H2399. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: Isaiah 38:17 describes God casting the speaker’s sins behind his back. This image expresses forgiveness alongside Hezekiah’s rescue from death.

words.label: Babylon
words.greekNote: This form comes from verse 1. Later verses use other word forms and names for the people.
words.meaning: The city and kingdom of the visitors. Isaiah also names Babylon in his warning about the future.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H894. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: Babylon sends a gift in Isaiah 39:1, but becomes the destination of Judah’s lost treasures in verse 6. The warning concerns the same wealth Hezekiah showed the visitors.

words.label: Eunuchs
words.meaning: Court servants described with a term that can denote eunuchs or officials.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H5631. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: Isaiah 39:7 places Hezekiah’s descendants in the Babylonian king’s palace as servants. The warning reverses their position: members of Judah’s royal family will serve a foreign ruler.

words.label: Peace
words.meaning: Peace or well-being in Hezekiah’s days.
words.grammar: Hebrew dictionary entry H7965. The word shown is its dictionary form. Its spelling in the verse can differ.
words.discussion: In Isaiah 39:8, Hezekiah speaks of peace in his own days after hearing that his descendants will be taken away. His response contrasts present security with the future loss Isaiah announces.

words.label: Truth / stability
words.greekNote: Swete’s Greek uses δικαιοσύνη, which commonly means righteousness or justice. The Hebrew and Greek words do not have identical meanings.

guides.title: The Assyrian crisis
guides.description: Follow the Assyrian threat from Lachish to Jerusalem.

steps.title: Locate the two cities
steps.text: Find Lachish on the map. An Assyrian official travels from here to Jerusalem. The line connects the cities; the exact route is unknown.

steps.title: Listen to the argument
steps.text: The speaker challenges trust in Egypt and Hezekiah. How does he use these places to support his argument?

steps.title: A public audience
steps.text: The officials request Aramaic. The speaker addresses the people on the wall in their own language. Why does his choice matter?

steps.title: A threat to move the people
steps.text: Compare the offer of food and land with the promised removal to another land. How does the speech make submission sound attractive?

guides.title: Two accounts, one crisis
guides.description: Compare Isaiah’s account with Assyrian records.

steps.title: The palace viewpoint
steps.text: What does this image emphasize about the victorious king? What does it leave out?

steps.title: The royal inscription
steps.text: The Assyrian inscription presents the campaign as a royal victory. Compare its purpose with the biblical account.

steps.title: How the account ends
steps.text: Isaiah credits God with saving Jerusalem. Compare this explanation with the Assyrian account. Consider the purpose and limits of each source.

steps.title: Years between events
steps.text: The final verse describes a death many years later. Consecutive verses can describe events that are far apart in time.

guides.title: Babylon and Judah’s future
guides.description: Study the events before and after Isaiah 39.

steps.title: A vulnerable king
steps.text: Chapter 38 describes Hezekiah’s illness and a promise to defend Jerusalem. Chapter order alone does not establish the order of these events.

steps.title: Visitors from Babylon
steps.text: Babylon sends visitors to Hezekiah. Their visit’s exact date is uncertain. The map uses 703 BCE to show the setting.

steps.title: Jerusalem’s later destruction
steps.text: The timeline shows Jerusalem’s destruction in 587/586 BCE. Compare Isaiah’s warning about the palace treasures with this later event. Related authorship study: McClellan compares Isaiah 39’s warning with chapter 40’s perspective after exile. His video explains the term Second Isaiah.

steps.title: Persia takes Babylon
steps.text: The timeline ends with Cyrus’s conquest. The Cyrus Cylinder gives a royal account. It does not mention the return of Judah’s exiles.

guides.title: Worship and justice
guides.description: Trace care for vulnerable people across Isaiah.

steps.title: Learn to do good
steps.text: Read Isaiah 1:10–20. Compare the criticism of worship with the command to defend vulnerable people.

steps.title: The vineyard
steps.text: Read Isaiah 5:1–7. Identify the fruit the vineyard owner expected and what he received.

steps.title: The chosen fast
steps.text: Read Isaiah 58:3–12. Name the actions that make worship visible in daily life.

guides.title: Comfort and return
guides.description: Follow images of strength, remembrance, and renewed belonging.

steps.title: Strength for the weary
steps.text: Read Isaiah 40:27–31. Notice how the reply addresses the complaint that God does not see the people.

steps.title: Zion remembered
steps.text: Read Isaiah 49:14–18. Compare Zion’s complaint with the images in God’s answer.

steps.title: A covenant of peace
steps.text: Read Isaiah 54:7–17. Consider how the promise answers abandonment and fear.

guides.title: Read the servant passages
guides.description: Compare the servant’s work, suffering, and vindication.

steps.title: Justice without crushing
steps.text: Read Isaiah 42:1–9. Describe the servant’s task and manner. Keep questions of identity separate from these observations.

steps.title: A wider mission
steps.text: Read Isaiah 49:1–6. Notice how the passage names Israel and also describes restoring Israel.

steps.title: Suffering and vindication
steps.text: Read Isaiah 52:13 through 53:12. Track the speakers and how their view of the servant changes. Compare Christian interpretation in LDS mode.
